power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: A Three-Wave RI-CLPM Linking Adolescent Affect and their Engagement with Sustainable Development
keywords: Conceptualization, Formal Analysis, Data Curation, Writing-Original Draft, Writing-Review & Editing, Visualization. SF: Investigation, Data Curation. PM: Conceptualization, Methodology, Resources, Supervision, Project Administration, Funding Acquisition, Writing -Review & Editing Affect

text.text: This study examines reciprocal relationships between affect and engagement and disengagement with sustainable development in a cohort of 580 Portuguese adolescents assessed serendipitously before COVID-19 (ages 12-13), during lockdown (ages 13-14), and approximately one year after lockdown (ages 13-14).
Random-intercept cross-lagged panel modelling (RI-CLPM) distinguished stable between-person differences from within-person fluctuations.
Adolescents with higher negative affect generally reported lower engagement and higher disengagement.
Within individuals, higher-than-usual negative affect before the pandemic predicted greater subsequent disengagement during lockdown.
In turn, higher-thanusual negative affect during lockdown predicted greater subsequent engagement.
No crosslagged effects involving positive affect or from engagement or disengagement to affect were statistically significant.
The findings suggest that negative affect may precede different responses to sustainable development across contextual conditions.

Efforts to promote engagement should therefore consider adolescents' emotional experiences alongside their circumstances, rather than assume that negative affect necessarily undermines engagement or that evoking it will encourage sustainable action.

Over the past three decades, the constructs of engagement and disengagement -which both broadly capture qualities of an individual's subjective experiences of, and interactions with, aspects of their external environments -have been widely applied to the fields of educational (Fredricks et al., 2004; Reschly & Christenson, 2022; Wang, Degol, et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2024) and organizational psychology (Kahn, 1990; Rich et al., 2010; Shuck et al., 2013) due to their potential to address issues such as work absenteeism (Neuber et al., 2022), school dropout (Fall & Roberts, 2012) and problem behaviors (Wang & Fredricks, 2014).

text.text: Importantly, according to Prinzing, these findings were more consistent with the hypothesis that pro-environmental behavior promotes well-being through the satisfaction of basic psychological needs for competence, autonomy and relatedness than through "warm glow" alone.

This possibility is consistent with self-determination theory (Ryan & Deci, 2017) and earlier proposals that sustainable behavior may support autonomy, competence, and relatedness and thereby enhance well -being (Kasser, 2009).

text.text: Despite evidence that ESD can promote positive affect, there are also plausible circumstances where ESD may decrease positive affect or increase negative affect.
As noted by Venhoeven et al. (2013), certain pro-sustainable behaviors associated with ESD may be less inherently pleasurable and have a hedonic cost compared to nonsustainable alternatives.

text.text: For instance, individuals may find vegan meals less pleasant than non-vegan options, and turning down the thermostat during winter for energy conservation may be perceived as less pleasant than keeping the house warm.
This has contributed to the common perceptions that sustainable living requires personal sacrifice that can pose a threat to overall life quality (Brown & Kasser, 2005).

text.text: Importantly, however, the affective consequences of ESD may not be uniformly positive or negative, and may simultaneously have rewarding and aversive components.

Consistent with this possibility, in a cross-sectional study using the Youth Engagement in Global Sustainability Scale, youth engagement was significantly positively associated with positive affect but essentially unrelated to negative affect (Moreira, 2021).

text.text: This suggests that higher ESD may be accompanied by greater positive affect without a corresponding reduction in negative affect, which is consistent with the view that positive and negative affect are related but separable dimensions (Larsen et al., 2017; Tellegen et al., 1999).

text.text: To summarize, mixed research findings within the available literature suggest the relationship between affect and ESD/DSD is complex (Brosch, 2021; Brosch & Steg, 2021; Schneider et al., 2021).

text.text: On the one hand, people who experience more positive affect may be better equipped psychologically to engage with the global challenge of sustainable development.
On the other hand, negative affect, and particularly negative emotional reactions when confronted with the negative consequences of unsustainable practices, can also drive ESD.
In turn, while ESD may lead to positive affective experiences because it is intrinsically rewarding, it may also lead to negative experience if it implies self-sacrifice.

However, it remains unclear whether fluctuations in positive and negative affect within adolescents precede subsequent fluctuations in ESD or DSD, or whether these associations operate in the reverse direction.
Understanding these dynamics requires an integrative perspective that considers reciprocal interactions between individual, cultural/social and environmental processes.

Social-cognitive theories of personality, for example, conceptualize behavior as emerging dynamically from interactions between psychologically meaningful features of situations and internal cognitive-affective processes, including affect, goals, expectations, and situational appraisals (Cervone, 2023; Mischel, 2009; Mischel & Shoda, 1995).

text.text: Related perspectives in grounded and situated cognition similarly emphasize that cognition does not occur independently of bodily states and environmental context, but is embedded within ongoing interactions between the person and their surroundings (Barsalou, 2008; Clark, 2013).

text.text: Importantly, affect is not merely an outcome of these processes: substantial evidence indicates that affective states can themselves influence judgment, interpretation, and even perceptual construal of external stimuli (Clore & Palmer, 2009; Siegel et al., 2018).

text.text: From this perspective, ESD and DSD can be conceptualized as dynamically expressed states that may fluctuate not only with affective experience but also with changes in the broader social and environmental context.

The COVID-19 pandemic provides a particularly informative contextual discontinuity in this regard: pre-pandemic, lockdown, and subsequent periods involved markedly different social and environmental conditions that may have altered how adolescents interpreted and responded to sustainability-related challenges.

In a longitudinal study of Portuguese adolescents, Pedras et al. (2024) found that the positive association between pre-pandemic subjective well-being and ESD during lockdown was weaker among adolescents who more strongly understood COVID-19 as a consequence of human-nature interactions.

(2024)</ref> found that the positive association between pre-pandemic subjective well-being and ESD during lockdown was weaker among adolescents who more strongly understood COVID-19 as a consequence of human-nature interactions.

text.text: This finding suggests that adolescents' interpretations of a shared crisis may be relevant to the relationship between their internal experiences and ESD.
However, this study focused on subjective well-being as a composite of cognitive and emotional indicators, leaving unclear the distinct contributions of positive and negative affect.
Moreover, the study ended during lockdown and did not distinguish stable between-person differences from withinperson fluctuations.
The present study extends this work using data from the same longitudinal project, including a third assessment approximately one year after the onset of the pandemic.
We focus specifically on positive and negative affect as separate dimensions, examining whether each precedes, or follows, changes in ESD and DSD.

Using RI-CLPM, we distinguish between-person differences from within-person fluctuations and examine these prospective associations across two successive intervals, without assuming that the pattern observed from before the pandemic to lockdown also characterizes the subsequent interval.

In terms of hypothesized relations between affect and ESD/DSD, at the between-person level prior research led us to anticipate that (1) positive affect would be positively associated with ESD and negatively associated with DSD; and (2) negative affect would be positively associated with DSD and negatively associated with ESD .

Given the lack of prior research specifically testing longitudinal associations between affect and ESD or DSD, and given the apparent complexity of their causal associations, we did not make specific predictions regarding within-person lagged effects.
Data are from a longitudinal study on student engagement with sustainable development in Portuguese schools that ran from 2019 to 2021.
For this broader study, we recruited participants from approximately 150 middle schools and mixed-grade schools across the Northern, Central, and Lisbon regions.
All seventh-grade students from these schools were invited to join the study, ensuring diverse student demographics.
In Portugal, the age of entry to 7 th grade is 12 years old.

text.text: The main analytic sample for this specific study consisted of adolescents who completed surveys in the final semester of 7 th (May-June 2019), 8 th (May-June 2020), and 9th grades (May-June 2021) with at least a 75% response rate for all surveys.

text.text: To determine the most appropriate model for our longitudinal data we first compared several SEM models including a baseline stability model, a cross-lagged panel model (CLPM), and a random-intercept CLPM (RI-CLPM).

text.text: First, for each variable a randomintercept was specified as a latent factor, with each having as its indicators the three repeated observed scores for ESD, DSD, PA and NA affect, respectively.
All factorloadings on the random-intercepts were fixed to 1.
Second, observed scores within waves were each regressed on a within-person latent variable (within-person residual), also with the factor-loading fixed to 1.
Autoregressive and cross-lagged regressive effects between these within-person residuals were freely estimated.
In a second ancillary RI-CLPM, we fixed the covariances between residuals of within -person centered variables to equality.

text.text: The objective of this longitudinal study was to examine the reciprocal relationships between human affect and ESD/DSD over time.
To achieve this objective, we analyzed data from the same sample of adolescents over three years.

Serendipitously, data collection at T1 occurred before the COVID -19 pandemic, data collection at T2 occurred during an early lockdown period of the COVID -19 pandemic, and data collection at T3 occurred approximately one year after the onset of the pandemic.
As such, each data collection moment coincided with markedly different social contexts.

Using a RI-CLPM approach, we were able to separate between-person differences from within-person processes; that is, whether changes in adolescents' affect or ESD/DSD relative to their own typical level predicted subsequent changes in other constructs.

Importantly, because these within-person fluctuations occurred across data collection moments characterized by substantially different social and environmental conditions, their interpretation should also be considered in relation to the broader context in which they emerged.

This considered, we focus our discussion on results concerning the central research question of this article (How do affect and ESD influence one another over time?) before discussing study strengths and limitations.
A first finding concerned the direction of the longitudinal relationship between affect and ESD/DSD.
Overall, the within-person results suggested that affect more consistently preceded subsequent changes in ESD/DSD than ESD/DSD preceded changes in affect.

This pattern is consistent with emerging longitudinal evidence showing that within-person increases in positive and negative affect can prospectively predict subsequent environmentally relevant behavior, whereas reciprocal effects from green behavior to later affect are often weaker or absent over longer measurement intervals (Stein et al., 2025 (Stein et al., , 2026)).

text.text: Such findings are compatible with theoretical perspectives that position affect as an antecedent of cognition and action: positive affect may broaden cognitive and behavioral repertoires and support adaptive, futureoriented behavior, whereas negative affect can narrow attention toward more immediate concerns (Fredrickson, 2001).

text.text: A second major finding emerged when specifically examining prospective relationships from pre-pandemic (T1) to pandemic lockdown (T2).
The analysis showed that within-person deviations in negative affect at T1 were positively and significantly related to subsequent within-person deviations in DSD at T2.
Put more simply, adolescents who experienced higher negative affect than was typical for them at T1 subsequently reported higher-than-expected levels of DSD during the pandemic.

The model also presented tentative evidence that adolescents experiencing higher-thanexpected positive affect at T1 subsequently reported higher-than-expected ESD during the pandemic, although this effect did not remain statistically significant under the adjusted α level used to control familywise Type I error.

One plausible interpretation of these findings, as we hypothesized in the introduction, is that adolescents' affective functioning prior to the pandemic shaped their capacity to respond adaptively when confronted with the substantial disruption and uncertainty that followed.

This interpretation is consistent with broaden -and-build theory, according to which positive emotional experiences broaden cognitive and behavioral repertoires and, over time, contribute to the development of enduring psychological and coping resources that can subsequently be drawn upon during adversity (Fredrickson, 2001) .

text.text: Prospective studies support this resource-building function of positive affect: positive emotions have been shown to predict subsequent increases in broad-minded coping and psychological resilience (Cohn et al., 2009; Fredrickson & Joiner, 2002) , while research conducted around major unforeseen crises suggests that such pre-existing affective resources can contribute to more resilient responses when adversity occurs (Fredrickson et al., 2003).

text.text: Evidence from environmental psychology provides more specific support for this interpretation.
Recent longitudinal research has found that positive affect predicts greater subsequent pro-environmental behavior, whereas negative affect can predict reduced subsequent engagement.

For example, higher-than-usual positive affect has been shown to predict subsequent increases in proactive and citizenship green behavior in multi-wave RI-CLPM studies (Stein et al., 2026), while anticipated positive affect has similarly been found to predict greater subsequent engagement in proenvironmental behavior (Strömbäck et al., 2025) .

text.text: Particularly relevant to the present study, Stein et al. (2026) also found that within-person increases in negative affect predicted subsequent increases in counterproductive green behavior.

text.text: Thus, although the present study assessed general rather than environmentally specific affect, its within-person findings converge with emerging evidence that elevated negative affect can, under some circumstances, precede environmental disengagement.
A third major finding emerged when examining prospective relationships from pandemic lockdown period (T2) to approximately 1-year later (T3).
Within-person deviations in negative affect at T2 were positively and significantly related to subsequent within-person deviations in ESD at T3.
Thus, adolescents who experienced higher negative affect than was typical for them in the first months of the pandemic subsequently reported higher-than-expected levels of ESD.

The model also provided tentative evidence that higher-than-usual positive affect at T2 was associated with greater subsequent DSD, although this effect did not remain statistically significant under the adjusted α level used to control familywise Type I error.

Taken together, these findings point to a prospective role for elevated negative affect and raise the possibility that comparatively poorer affective well-being during this particular period of global crisis, may, under some circumstances, have contributed to later ESD.

Although this finding may be interpreted as contradicting our initial expectation that positive affect would facilitate ESD through processes such as 'broaden-and-build' (Fredrickson, 2001), growing evidence suggests that negative affective experiences may also be a driver of ESD.

text.text: This may be particularly relevant to the context in which the present within-person effect emerged.
Evidence indicates the first months of the COVID-19 pandemic were characterized by substantial disruption and negative emotional experiences among young people.
For example, Lawrance et al. (2022) found that young people associated the pandemic particularly with anxiety, frustration, isolation, disconnection, loss, and concern about their future.

text.text: Importantly, there is also empirical evidence that experiences of the pandemic became linked to environmental concerns and sustainability-related responses.

text.text: Similarly, Daryanto et al. (Daryanto et al., 2022) found that individuals who more strongly attributed the pandemic to excessive human intrusion into nature reported greater environmental awareness, which was in turn associated with more pro-environmental behavior.

text.text: Although based on overlapping data, this finding identifies adolescents' interpretations of the pandemic as a possible consideration when explaining the present results.
Negative affect during lockdown may have accompanied concerns that encouraged subsequent ESD, although the present analysis did not test these appraisals or their role in the observed association.
The longitudinal design of this study, and the relatively large sample sourced from multiple schools across Portugal increases confidence of the internal validity of the results.

Confidence in the findings, and particularly within-person inferences, is also enhanced by our finding of strong scale reliability at each moment, moderate-to-low ICCs, the conservative adjusted alpha to control for Type I error, and the observation of at least weak longitudinal measurement invariance across variables.
Nonetheless, we acknowledge the study has several limitations, which we shall consider in turn.

First, we acknowledge that in the pursuit of testing specific associations and with the aim to having parsimonious and easy-to-interpret models we did not consider demographic variables (e.g. sex) and therefore their potential confounding effects in the analyses.
Future studies could consider incorporating such variables into the CLPM and RI-CLPM analyses to test whether they have impact on the cross-lagged effects reported in this study.
Another limitation related specifically to the CLPM and RI-CLPM analyses was that we did not incorporate measurement models.

Estimating measurement models for each wave-specific assessment of affect and ESD/DSD may provide more robust estimates of the cross-lagged effects, and therefore should be considered in future studies (although we caution that the large number of model parameters would necessitate a larger sample).
Second, it is important to consider aspects of the study design that can impact on the generalizability of the study results to the target population, which for this study was Portuguese adolescents.
The analytic sample included only adolescents who participated at all three assessments and met the response-completeness criterion.
Selective retention may therefore have influenced the observed associations, limiting their generalizability to the original cohort.
We also note that the sample comprised adolescents enrolled in just one academic year.
As such, it is unclear whether the same findings would emerge if adolescents from a different academic year had also been followed.

Thirdly, the availability of a longitudinal dataset tracking adolescents from preto post-COVID19 serendipitously provided an opportunity to understand how affective experiences during the first months of the pandemic, when a global crisis linked to unsustainable human actions was undeniably very salient, shaped people's experiences and interactions with the topic of sustainable development.

However, this specific historical context may mean that our findings, and thus our conclusions about the longitudinal associations between affect and ESD/DSD may not generalize to more normative circumstances.

We also note that the pandemic required different data collection methods to be used at T1 (paper surveys in classrooms) and T2/T3 (online surveys during online classes), which could contribute to variations in the observed relationships and should be considered when interpreting the results.

Overall, this longitudinal RI-CLPM study shows that affective experiences may play a role in shaping people's interactions with, and experiences of, sustainable development, and therefore are an important factor to consider in efforts to promote ESD and/or reduce DSD.
More specifically, the study showed that when adolescents experienced higher negative affect than was typical for them during the COVID lockdown, this was followed by increases in subsequent ESD.
Thus, negative affect during an environmental or social crises, although unpleasant, may in some circumstances motivate adaptive responses.
At the same time, the study also showed that when adolescents experienced higher negative affect than expected before COVID, this was followed by increases in DSD during lockdown.
Thus, the study seems to suggest that whether elevated negative affect precedes ESD or DSD depends on the context in which it is experienced.

Thus, aligning with Schneider et al. (Schneider et al., 2021), we caution against rushing to apply interventions that seek to promote ESD by evoking emotions, as the outcomes may vary as a function on when the intervention is applied.
